title: Why do some heavy things float?
outcome: The student will explain that floating depends on density (mass per unit volume) compared to water, not just weight.
subject: physics

concepts.title: Why do some heavy things float?
concepts.centralCause: An object floats if its average density is less than the density of water (1 g/cm3) and sinks if it is greater.
conditions: The body is uniform and has no hidden cavities (unless specified)
The body does not soak up water or dissolve
The body is in ordinary fresh water
The body is not held by any external force

cards.title: Weight vs. Density

fact.statement: Whether an object sinks depends on its density, which is how much mass is packed into a specific volume.
conditions: The body is in still water
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, sections 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure and 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: Can a giant ship made of heavy steel float while a tiny pebble sinks?
hook.predictPrompt: The ship weighs thousands of tons, the pebble just a few grams. So why could the heavy one float and the light one sink? Guess, and say why you think so.

cards.explanation: Density is a measure of how 'crowded' the atoms are inside an object. It is calculated by dividing mass by volume. A heavy object might float if it takes up a huge amount of space, making its density lower than water.

action.instruction: Picture a big wooden block and a small chip cut from it. Before you drop the chip in: will it sink or float? Then compare it with the big block.

question.prompt: If you have a huge piece of cork and a small piece of cork, which one will float? Explain why.

key.expectedCause: Both will float because they are made of the same material with the same density.
acceptable: Both float because cork is less dense than water
key.typicalMistake: The big one floats because it is bigger.
key.followUp: Does the size of the object change its density if the material stays the same?

cards.title: The Rule of 1 g/cm3

fact.statement: Water has a density of 1 g/cm3. Objects with a density higher than 1 g/cm3 sink.
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, sections 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure and 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: Why does a small stone sink but a big piece of wood float?
hook.predictPrompt: A small stone sinks, a big log floats. What do you think the water is "checking" when it decides? Guess, and say why.

cards.explanation: To see if something floats, we compare it to water. If an object's density is greater than 1 g/cm3, it is 'heavier' for its size than water is, so it sinks. If it is less, it floats.

action.instruction: Every cubic centimetre of stone weighs 2 g, of wood 0.6 g, of water 1 g. Guess which one sinks, then compare each with the same amount of water.
constants: we compare one cubic centimetre of each

cards.title: Cutting the Stone

fact.statement: Cutting a uniform object in half keeps its density the same.
conditions: The body does not soak up water
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, sections 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure and 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: If you cut a sinking stone in half, will the halves still sink?
hook.predictPrompt: Will both halves still sink? Guess, and say why.

cards.explanation: Density is a property of the material. When you cut an object, you reduce its mass and its volume by the same proportion. Because both mass and volume change together, the density stays the same.

action.instruction: Picture a stone that sinks. Cut it in half in your head. Did each cubic centimetre of stone get any lighter? Guess, then compare a half with the whole stone.

question.prompt: A candle floats in water. You cut it into ten thin slices and drop them in. What happens to each slice, and why?

key.expectedCause: Every slice still floats: cutting makes the mass and the volume smaller by the same share, so each slice has the same density as the whole candle, and that is less than water.
acceptable: Slices float because the wax is the same, cutting does not change how heavy each cubic centimetre is.
If a slice has an air bubble or a metal wick holder, it may behave differently.
key.typicalMistake: Thin slices are lighter so they float better — or they are small so they sink.
key.followUp: Did cutting change how much one cubic centimetre of wax weighs?

criteria.example: Yes, because the density stays the same.

cards.title: The Secret of the Ship

fact.statement: Hollow bodies float because the air inside lowers their average density.
conditions: The body does not soak up water
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, sections 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure and 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: How can a massive steel ship float while a small piece of steel sinks?
hook.predictPrompt: What if the ship's hull filled up with water? Guess what happens, and say why.

cards.explanation: A ship is hollow. When we calculate its average density, we include the air inside. Because the air is very light, the average density of the whole ship becomes less than the density of water.

action.instruction: Put an empty plastic bottle with the cap on into a bowl of water. Guess what happens, then fill it with water, close it and try again.

cards.title: The Density Challenge

fact.statement: To predict if an object floats, calculate its density (mass/volume) and compare it to 1 g/cm3.
conditions: The body does not soak up water
fact.source: Facts cross-checked against OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, sections 14.1 Fluids, Density, and Pressure and 14.4 Archimedes' Principle and Buoyancy (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); notes written in our own words, no OpenStax text included — https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/14-4-archimedes-principle-and-buoyancy

hook.question: Can you predict which objects will float without seeing them?
hook.predictPrompt: If you only know how heavy something is and how much space it takes up, can you tell whether it floats? Guess how, and say why.

cards.explanation: To solve any floating problem, find the density. Divide the mass by the volume. If the result is less than 1 g/cm3, it floats. If it is more, it sinks.

action.instruction: Object A: 400 g, takes up 500 cm³. Object B: 150 g, takes up 100 cm³. Guess which one floats, then work out how many grams fit into each cubic centimetre.
constants: water: 1 g in every cubic centimetre

question.prompt: A toy weighs 90 g and takes up 100 cm³. A bolt weighs only 80 g but takes up 10 cm³. Which one floats, and how did you decide?

key.expectedCause: The toy floats: 90 g in 100 cm³ is 0.9 g per cubic centimetre, less than water. The bolt sinks: 80 g in 10 cm³ is 8 g per cubic centimetre, more than water. The lighter bolt sinks because its mass is packed into a small space.
acceptable: The toy is lighter than the same amount of water, the bolt is heavier than the same amount of water.
If the toy is hollow and leaks, it could fill with water.
key.typicalMistake: The bolt is lighter, so it floats.
key.followUp: How much would 10 cm³ of water weigh, compared with the bolt?

criteria.example: A floats because 0.8 is less than 1. B sinks because 1.5 is more than 1.
